title: CLAUDE.md
text:
This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.


# Preview site locally
quarto preview

# Build site (output goes to docs/)
quarto render

# Convert publications.xlsx to publications.yml (runs automatically on render)
python xlsx_to_yml.py

# Install Python dependency for xlsx conversion (one-time)
pip install openpyxl
The built site lives in docs/ — GitHub Pages is configured to serve from that directory.



This is a Quarto academic website. The source .qmd files render to static HTML in docs/. Navigation and global settings are controlled entirely by _quarto.yml.



_quarto.yml — site-wide config: navbar, footer, theme, analytics. Comment/uncomment entries here to show/hide pages.
index.qmd — homepage
people.qmd — team page; pulls data from YAML files in people/
pub-listing.qmd — auto-generated publications page; reads publications.yml via the pub-listing.ejs template and pub-listing.css
publications.qmd — manually curated publications page
projects.qmd — grants/projects page (currently commented out of the navbar)
posts.qmd — listing page for all posts (filtered by #category=news, #category=paper, etc.)
remove-stray-divfence.lua — Lua filter that strips stray ::: artifacts produced by the EJS listing template











Content type
Source




Team members
people/*.yml (one file per role: pi.yml, researcher.yml, phd-student.yml, etc.)


Publications
publications.xlsx → auto-converted to publications.yml via xlsx_to_yml.py


Grants/projects
projects.yml


Posts (news, papers, events, presentations)
posts/<post-folder>/index.qmd with YAML frontmatter categories: [news|paper|event|presentation]






Each person entry follows this pattern (indented under a list, no top-level key):
   - path: https://personal-website-or-linkedin.com
     image: "/files/profiles/photo.jpg"
     title: "Full Name"
     subtitle: "Role"
     categories: [Role Category]
     started: "2023"
     ended: "ongoing"   # use "ongoing" for current members
Profile images go in files/profiles/. The people.qmd listing controls which role files are included and whether alumni appear.




Edit publications.xlsx (columns: Section, Authors, Year, Date, Title, Paper Link, Journal, Volume, Issue, Pages, DOI + optional PDF, GitHub, Code, Data, Categories, etc.)
python xlsx_to_yml.py converts it to publications.yml (runs automatically before quarto render)
Use Section: Selected Work or Section: Peer-reviewed Journal Paper to place entries in the correct section of pub-listing.qmd




To temporarily remove a page from the navbar, comment out its entry in _quarto.yml under website.navbar.left. Example pattern already used in the file:
# - text: Grants
#   href: projects.qmd



New posts go in posts/<post-slug>/index.qmd. Set categories in frontmatter to route the post to the correct navbar filter (news, paper, event, presentation). The draft: true frontmatter key hides a post; draft-mode: unlinked (set in posts/_metadata.yml) means drafts are built but not linked from listings.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: Introduction (1/2)
text:
Introduction (1/2)
This guide, written by the Coding Group of the ONDA Lab, is a humorous collection of bad programming habits. While many guides explain how to write good code, we realized that another way to learn is by looking at what not to do.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: Introduction (2/2)
text:
Introduction (2/2)
After all, most of us (certainly we, at least) are naturally prone to becoming bad programmers. So instead of only focusing on the “right” way, this guide highlights the habits you really shouldn’t have (but probably already do).

Enjoy!

P.S. If you think we’re writing this because we’re excellent programmers, you couldn’t be more wrong. But we’re trying to unlearn these bad habits!


 P.P.S. Click here to   download the PDF version 📄

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 1. Write your code as a single long script
text:
1. Write your code as a single long script

The truth: unless you have a very short task, a very long script is often difficult to work on, to reuse, to mantain, and to share.

When you write long script you tend to think in a less modular way and you don’t break down you problem.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 2. Create numerous versions of your code using v1, v2, v3, etc.
text:
2. Create numerous versions of your code using v1, v2, v3, etc.

The truth: manually versioning files leads to chaos. You end up with analysis_v1.R, analysis_v2_final.R, analysis_v2_final_REAL.R, and no idea which one is actually current — or what changed between them.

Use version control (e.g. Git) instead. Every change is tracked, timestamped, and reversible — without a graveyard of files cluttering your folder.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 3. Don’t think before coding—just jump in and write lines of code based on instinct.
text:
3. Don’t think before coding—just jump in and write lines of code based on instinct.

The truth: coding without a plan often means solving the wrong problem, or building something that needs to be completely rewritten once the real structure becomes clear.

A few minutes spent thinking about inputs, outputs, and the steps in between saves hours of untangling spaghetti code later.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 4. Spend days and days in designing how you would code, before actually coding.
text:
4. Spend days and days in designing how you would code, before actually coding.

The truth: over-planning is just procrastination in disguise. You can’t anticipate every problem until you start writing real code, and a perfect design on paper rarely survives contact with reality.

Design just enough to start, then iterate. The code itself will show you what you didn’t think of.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 5. If you need to reuse code throughout your analysis, copy and paste as much as possible.
text:
5. If you need to reuse code throughout your analysis, copy and paste as much as possible.

The truth: copy-pasted code means that when you find a bug — and you will — you have to hunt it down in every single copy. You will always miss at least one.

Write a function instead. Fix the logic once, and every caller benefits automatically. Your future self will thank you.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 6. Do not waste time on writing comments in your code.
text:
6. Do not waste time on writing comments in your code.

The truth: code you wrote six months ago might as well have been written by a stranger. Without any comments, you’ll spend more time re-understanding your own work than writing new code.

But don’t explain what the code does — explain why. A good comment captures intent and hidden constraints, not mechanics that the code already shows.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 7. Use the shortest possible names for your objects and functions.
text:
7. Use the shortest possible names for your objects and functions.

The truth: x, tmp, df2, f — these names say absolutely nothing. The next time you open the file (or someone else does), you’ll have no idea what any of it means.

Names are free documentation. patient_age_at_baseline is always better than pab. If the name needs a comment to explain it, the name is wrong.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 8. Always write functions that are absolutely generalizable.
text:
8. Always write functions that are absolutely generalizable.

The truth: building a perfectly general-purpose function for a one-off task is over-engineering. It takes longer to write, harder to test, and more often than not, it never gets reused.

Write for the problem in front of you. You can generalize later, if and when you actually need to. “You Aren’t Gonna Need It” is a principle, not an excuse to be lazy.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 9. When using comments, comment in detail every single step.
text:
9. When using comments, comment in detail every single step.

The truth: over-commenting clutters the code and makes it harder to read. A comment that just restates what the code obviously does adds noise, not signal.

# add 1 to i above i <- i + 1 is not a comment — it’s pollution. Save your comments for the non-obvious parts: the edge case, the workaround, the invariant that isn’t obvious from the code alone.

title: How to Write Terrible Code
section: 10. Don’t use AI, but solve every problem by hand
text:
10. Don’t use AI, but solve every problem by hand

The truth: refusing to use AI tools when they’re available is like refusing to use a calculator. It slows you down on routine tasks and leaves less mental energy for the parts that actually require thinking.

But don’t outsource your thinking entirely either. If you can’t read, understand, and explain the code AI wrote for you, you don’t own it — and you won’t be able to fix it when it breaks.

title: ONDA Lab website
text:
Lab
  

  
  
Welcome to the website of the ONDA Lab (Open methodologies in Neurorehabilitation and Data Analysis)
The Lab is located at IRCCS San Camillo in Venice its research focuses on Neurorehabilitation and in particular on: Neurophysiology, Neuropsychology, and Neuroscience.


The Lab philosophy is focused on rigour and Open Science principles. We are committed to sharing our code, methods, data, results but also teaching materials and educational resources to the scientific community, to promote transparency, reproducibility and collaboration in research.




We develop open tools for neuropsychological assessment and rehabilitation
We study brain functions and biomarkers using MEEG
We create open-source pipelines for neural data analysis
We develop/optimize methods for behavioural and brain data analysis
